lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
A furnace is the heart of any foundry. Without a reliable furnace, you cannot melt metal, and without melted metal, you cannot cast anything. In many African workshops, imported furnaces are expensive and hard to repair. Building your own furnace from locally available materials saves money, creates jobs, and gives you control over the melting process. This module teaches you how to construct a simple, effective furnace that burns charcoal, coke, or even waste oil. You will learn to build a furnace that reaches temperatures above 1200Â°Câhot enough to melt aluminium, brass, and bronze. With the right design, you can also melt cast iron at around 1400Â°C.

Why does this matter? Across Africa, metal casting supports agriculture, construction, and transport. Farmers need plough parts, water pumps, and grinding mills. Builders need window frames, door hinges, and roofing sheets. Transporters need engine parts and brake drums. Most of these items are imported. By building your own furnace, you can produce them locally, create income, and reduce dependence on imports. A well-built furnace can last for years if maintained properly.

The furnace you will build in this module is a simple shaft furnace, also called a cupola or a crucible furnace. It uses a steel drum or clay-lined pit as the body, a firebrick or clay lining to hold heat, a tuyere (air pipe) to blow air into the fire, and a grate to hold the fuel. You will use a hand-cranked blower, a vacuum cleaner motor, or a small electric fan to supply air. The fuel can be charcoal, coke, or even dry wood, but charcoal and coke give the best heat.

Before you start, understand that furnace building is not just about stacking bricks. You must control air flow, fuel size, and insulation. Too much air cools the furnace; too little air starves the fire. Wet fuel creates smoke and lowers temperature. A good furnace builder checks every detail. In the next lessons, you will learn the tools, materials, step-by-step method, common mistakes, safety rules, and finally build your own furnace in a practical exercise. By the end, you will have a working furnace and the skills to melt metal safely.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To build a furnace, you need basic tools and materials that are available in most African towns. You do not need expensive equipment. Start with a steel drum (200-litre oil drum) or a large metal bucket. If you cannot find a drum, you can dig a pit and line it with clay. You will also need firebricks or clay soil. Firebricks are best because they withstand high heat, but if they are not available, use termite mound clay or river clay mixed with sand. Avoid ordinary cement bricksâthey crack at high temperatures.

For the lining, you need a refractory mixture. A good recipe is 3 parts clay, 1 part sand, and 1 part wood ash or sawdust. The ash makes the lining porous and resistant to cracking. Mix with water until it is like thick mud. You will also need a tuyereâa metal pipe (about 2-3 cm diameter) that carries air into the furnace. A car exhaust pipe or galvanised pipe works well. For the air supply, use a hand-cranked blower from a blacksmith, a vacuum cleaner motor, or a 12V car heater fan. You will need a grate made from steel bars or a heavy metal mesh to hold the fuel and let ash fall through.

Other tools: a shovel for mixing clay, a bucket for water, a trowel or wooden float for shaping the lining, a hacksaw or angle grinder for cutting the drum and pipe, a measuring tape, and a marker. For safety, you need leather gloves, safety goggles, a face mask (for dust), and a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand. A wheelbarrow helps move materials. If you are using a steel drum, cut a hole near the bottom for the tuyere and a larger opening at the top for loading fuel and a crucible.

Gather everything before you start. Check that the drum is clean and free of oil or paintâburn it out first if necessary. Test your air supply: it should blow a steady stream of air. Make sure the clay is free of stones and roots. If you use firebricks, soak them in water before laying them so they bond well with the clay. A good furnace builder organises tools and materials in one place. This saves time and prevents accidents. In the next lesson, you will use these tools to build the furnace step by step.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Prepare the drum. If using a 200-litre steel drum, cut off the top lid with a hacksaw or angle grinder. Cut a 5 cm hole near the bottom for the tuyere. Also cut a 15 cm diameter hole in the side about 20 cm from the bottomâthis is the tap hole for removing slag and metal. Clean the inside with a wire brush. Burn out any paint or oil by building a small fire inside.

Step 2: Make the refractory lining. Mix 3 parts clay, 1 part sand, and 1 part wood ash. Add water slowly and mix with your feet or a shovel until it is thick and sticky. Let it rest for 30 minutes. Then apply a 5-8 cm thick layer inside the drum, starting from the bottom. Shape the bottom into a slight bowl so molten metal collects at the tap hole. Leave the tuyere hole open. Smooth the lining with wet hands. Allow it to dry for 2-3 days in the shade. If it cracks, fill the cracks with more clay mixture.

Step 3: Install the tuyere and grate. Insert a 2-3 cm diameter metal pipe through the tuyere hole, angled slightly downward. The pipe should reach about 10 cm inside the furnace. Seal around it with clay. Place a steel grate at the bottom, about 10 cm above the floor, to hold fuel and let ash fall. The grate can be made from 1 cm steel bars spaced 2 cm apart.

Step 4: Connect the air supply. Attach your blower or fan to the outer end of the tuyere with a hose or metal pipe. If using a vacuum cleaner motor, mount it on a wooden stand and connect with a flexible pipe. Test the air flowâit should be strong but not so strong that it blows ash out of the top.

Step 5: Cure the furnace. Build a small fire inside with charcoal and let it burn slowly for 2 hours. Then increase the fire gradually over another 2 hours. This drives out moisture and hardens the lining. Do not rushâfast heating causes cracks. After curing, your furnace is ready. Load charcoal or coke, light it, turn on the air, and in 15-20 minutes you can melt aluminium. For cast iron, use coke and preheat for 30 minutes. Always keep a lid or cover for the top to conserve heat.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Using ordinary cement or river sand without clay. Cement cracks at high temperatures and can explode. Fix: Use firebricks or a clay-sand-ash mixture. If you must use cement, mix it with fire clay (available at brick factories) and cure slowly.

Mistake 2: Too much air blast. Beginners often use a powerful fan that blows heat out of the furnace. The fire roars but the metal does not melt. Fix: Use a damper or a smaller fan. Aim for a gentle, steady blast. You can test by holding your hand near the tuyereâit should feel like a strong breeze, not a hurricane.

Mistake 3: Wet fuel. Charcoal or coke stored in the rain absorbs moisture. This lowers the temperature and creates steam. Fix: Store fuel under cover. Dry it in the sun for a day before use. If you hear hissing, the fuel is wet.

Mistake 4: Cracks in the lining. If the lining dries too fast or is too thin, it cracks. Fix: Dry slowly in shade, not in direct sun. Make the lining at least 5 cm thick. Repair cracks with fresh clay mixture and re-cure.

Mistake 5: No tap hole or blocked tap hole. Molten metal and slag need to flow out. If the tap hole is too small or clogged, you cannot pour. Fix: Make the tap hole 15 cm wide and keep it clear with a metal rod. Angle it downward so metal flows easily.

Mistake 6: Poor grate design. If the grate is too high, fuel does not sit in the hottest zone. If too low, ash blocks air. Fix: Place the grate 10 cm above the bottom. Use bars spaced 2 cm apart. Clean ash after every melt.

Mistake 7: Not preheating the furnace. Cold furnace walls absorb heat. Fix: Burn a small fire for 10-15 minutes before loading the main fuel. This also drives out moisture.

Mistake 8: Using a crucible that is too small or too thin. The crucible must hold enough metal and withstand heat. Fix: Use a clay-graphite crucible or make one from fire clay. Preheat it before use. Always use tongs to handle hot crucibles.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Furnace work is dangerous. Molten metal can burn you, fires can spread, and fumes can poison you. Follow these safety rules every time. First, wear the right gear: leather gloves, safety goggles, a face mask, long trousers, and closed leather boots. Never wear synthetic clothesâthey melt and stick to skin. Tie back long hair. Remove jewellery.

Second, work in a well-ventilated area. Carbon monoxide from charcoal and coke is deadly. Build your furnace outdoors or in a shed with open sides. Never work in a closed room. If you feel dizzy or sleepy, move to fresh air immediately. Keep a bucket of water and a fire extinguisher nearby. For metal fires, use dry sand or a CO2 extinguisherânever water on molten metal.

Third, handle fuel and fire carefully. Store charcoal and coke away from the furnace. Use a metal shovel to add fuel. Never use your hands. When lighting the furnace, use a long match or a gas torch. Do not pour petrol or kerosene on the fireâit can explode. Keep a safe distance when the furnace is running. The outside of the furnace gets very hot. Mark a 2-metre safety zone with stones or tape.

Fourth, prepare for spills. Place a sand tray under the tap hole to catch molten metal. Wear a leather apron. Use long-handled tongs to move the crucible. Never look directly into the furnace without gogglesâthe infrared light can damage your eyes. When pouring, stand to the side, not in front of the crucible. Pour slowly and steadily.

Fifth, maintain your furnace. Check the lining before every use. Repair cracks. Clean the grate and ash pit. Check the air pipe for blockages. A well-maintained furnace is a safe furnace. Teach everyone in your workshop these rules. Keep a first aid kit with burn cream and bandages. If someone gets burned, cool the area with clean water for 10 minutes and seek medical help. Never ignore a burn. Finally, work with a partner. Never melt metal alone. A partner can help in an emergency and watch for danger.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
In this exercise, you will build a small furnace using a 20-litre metal bucket or a small drum. This furnace will melt up to 2 kg of aluminium. Gather your tools and materials: a metal bucket, clay soil, sand, wood ash, water, a 1 cm metal pipe for the tuyere, a small grate, a hand-cranked blower or a 12V fan, and safety gear.

Step 1: Cut a 3 cm hole near the bottom of the bucket for the tuyere. Cut a 5 cm hole on the opposite side about 10 cm up for the tap hole. Clean the bucket.

Step 2: Mix the lining: 3 parts clay, 1 part sand, 1 part wood ash. Add water to make a thick mud. Apply a 4 cm layer inside the bucket, shaping the bottom into a bowl. Leave the tuyere and tap holes open. Smooth with wet hands. Let dry in shade for 2 days.

Step 3: Insert the tuyere pipe through the hole, angled down. Seal with clay. Place the grate 8 cm above the bottom. Connect the blower to the tuyere with a pipe or hose.

Step 4: Cure the furnace. Build a small charcoal fire inside. Burn gently for 1 hour, then increase for another hour. Let cool. Your furnace is ready.

Step 5: Test melt. Load charcoal to the top. Light it and turn on the air. After 10 minutes, place a small clay-graphite crucible with 1 kg of clean aluminium scrap into the furnace. Cover the top with a lid. In 15-20 minutes, the aluminium should be molten. Use long tongs to lift the crucible. Pour into a simple sand mould (a small hole in damp sand). Let it cool. You have cast your first metal part.

Record your results: How long did it take to melt? How much fuel did you use? Did the lining crack? If yes, repair and try again. Repeat the exercise until you can melt consistently. This small furnace is a training tool. Once you master it, you can scale up to a 200-litre drum furnace for production work. Remember: safety first, and always work with a partner.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a furnace in foundry work?
quiz.explanation: A furnace provides the heat needed to melt metal so it can be poured into moulds.

quiz.q: Which temperature is hot enough to melt aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium melts at about 660Â°C, so a furnace reaching 1200Â°C is more than sufficient.

quiz.q: What is a tuyere in a furnace?
options: B) A metal pipe that blows air into the fire
C) A tool for stirring molten metal
quiz.explanation: The tuyere is the air pipe that supplies oxygen to the fire for combustion.

quiz.q: Which material is best for lining a furnace?
quiz.explanation: Firebricks or a clay-sand-ash mixture withstand high temperatures without cracking.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using wet charcoal in a furnace?
options: B) It lowers the temperature and creates steam
C) It produces too much ash
quiz.explanation: Wet fuel absorbs heat to evaporate water, reducing the furnace temperature.

quiz.q: What is the correct mixing ratio for a refractory lining?
options: A) 1 part clay, 1 part sand, 1 part ash
B) 3 parts clay, 1 part sand, 1 part ash
C) 5 parts clay, 2 parts sand, 1 part ash
D) 2 parts clay, 2 parts sand, 1 part ash
quiz.explanation: The recommended ratio is 3:1:1 for clay, sand, and wood ash.

quiz.q: How long should you dry the furnace lining before curing?
quiz.explanation: Slow drying in shade for 2-3 days prevents cracks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the grate in a furnace?
options: A) To hold fuel and let ash fall through
quiz.explanation: The grate supports the fuel bed while allowing ash to drop out.

quiz.q: Why should you preheat a furnace before loading the main fuel?
options: B) To drive out moisture and warm the walls
C) To make the fire burn faster
quiz.explanation: Preheating removes moisture and prevents heat loss to cold walls.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using a powerful blower?
options: A) It cools the furnace too much
B) It blows heat out and wastes fuel
D) It makes the metal brittle
quiz.explanation: Too much air blast blows hot gases out, reducing efficiency.

quiz.q: How can you fix cracks in the furnace lining?
options: B) Fill with fresh clay mixture and re-cure
quiz.explanation: Repairing cracks with fresh clay mixture restores the lining.

quiz.q: What is the tap hole used for?
options: B) To let molten metal and slag flow out
quiz.explanation: The tap hole allows molten metal and slag to be removed from the furnace.

quiz.q: Why should you never pour water on a molten metal fire?
options: A) It makes the fire worse
B) It can cause an explosion
C) It cools the metal too fast
quiz.explanation: Water on molten metal can cause a violent steam explosion.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential for furnace work?
options: A) Leather gloves, goggles, face mask, boots
quiz.explanation: Leather gloves, goggles, face mask, and boots protect against burns and fumes.

quiz.q: Why is good ventilation important when using a charcoal furnace?
options: A) To keep the fire cool
B) To prevent carbon monoxide poisoning
D) To make the furnace last longer
quiz.explanation: Charcoal produces carbon monoxide, which is deadly in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What is the recommended safety zone around a running furnace?
quiz.explanation: A 2-metre zone keeps people safe from heat and spills.

quiz.q: How should you handle a hot crucible?
quiz.explanation: Long-handled tongs keep your hands away from the heat.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone gets a burn from molten metal?
options: B) Cool with clean water for 10 minutes and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Cooling with water reduces damage and medical help is necessary.

quiz.q: Why should you work with a partner when melting metal?
options: B) For emergency help and safety
quiz.explanation: A partner can assist in case of accidents and watch for dangers.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a small furnace from a metal bucket?
options: B) Cut holes for tuyere and tap hole
quiz.explanation: You must cut the tuyere and tap holes before lining the bucket.

quiz.q: How thick should the refractory lining be in a small bucket furnace?
quiz.explanation: A 4 cm lining provides enough insulation for small melts.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of wood ash in the refractory mixture?
options: B) To make it porous and resistant to cracking
quiz.explanation: Ash creates porosity that helps the lining withstand thermal expansion.

quiz.q: How long should you cure a small furnace with a gentle fire?
options: B) 1 hour, then increase for another hour
quiz.explanation: Gradual heating over 2 hours drives out moisture without cracking.

quiz.q: What type of crucible is recommended for melting aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Clay-graphite crucibles withstand high temperatures and thermal shock.

quiz.q: Why should you preheat the crucible before use?
options: B) To prevent thermal shock and cracking
quiz.explanation: Preheating gradually warms the crucible, reducing the risk of cracking.

quiz.q: What should you do after every melt to maintain the furnace?
options: A) Clean ash and check lining
quiz.explanation: Cleaning ash and checking for cracks keeps the furnace safe and efficient.

quiz.q: Which fuel gives the highest temperature in a foundry furnace?
quiz.explanation: Coke burns hotter and longer than charcoal or wood.

quiz.q: What is the danger of looking directly into a hot furnace without goggles?
options: B) Infrared light can damage eyes
quiz.explanation: Infrared radiation from the furnace can harm your eyes.

quiz.q: How can you test if your air blast is too strong?
options: B) Ash and sparks blow out of the top
quiz.explanation: Excessive air blows ash and heat out, indicating too much blast.

quiz.q: What is the final step of the practical exercise?
options: B) Test melt aluminium and pour into a mould
quiz.explanation: The exercise ends with melting and casting a small aluminium part.
